dispute, there are four areas of disagreement.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The most important is that we know that aggregate income is significantly under-reported to the I.R.S. Piketty and his co-authors estimate under-reporting from I.R.S. audits and then assign that income proportionately to reported income. Auten and Splinter say that’s empirically wrong and that under-reported income is more evenly distributed. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I am pretty sure the latter are correct about this point, but I’m much less confident that I agree with them on the other three, which have to do with allocating retained corporate earnings, attributing government spending, and how to account for the fact that higher-income tax units contain more married couples.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You see similar issues in other areas. As Noah Smith mentions in his recent </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4e30786a-f0a9-4430-8d62-1931c2e6a270?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">reconsideration of the neo-Brandeisian movement</a><span> in the United States, while these people are at heart </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/54edaf43-a25f-46c5-9333-40fc2313ee77?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">deeply ideological</a><span>, they gained credibility from a very real line of empirical research indicating that there had been a broad rise in market concentration and markups. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Probably the most influential paper in this literature is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bce8ceca-aa1e-4039-a644-bca678f256c3?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">this one by Jan De Loecker and Jan Eeckhout</a><span>, but there are many others. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>After the initial wave of “omg concentration!” papers came out, though, there was a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d606b98b-51a5-4d08-9cf4-a2f2cdbfc8d9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">counter-wave of contrary empirical findings</a><span>. In this case, it is deeply unclear to me which side is correct. As a political matter, I don’t think we should empower people like Barry Lynn and Matt Stoller who clearly don’t even care about the empirical evidence. But the empirical dispute itself is in fact important. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s also worth keeping in mind the structural incentives of academia. If concentration and markups aren’t increasing and nobody is saying that they are increasing, then an empirical paper saying “everything is fine” is going to be extremely boring. A smart academic isn’t going to waste time on that. Eventually someone comes along with an </span><em>interesting</em><span> finding and that gets published and then it creates a wave of followup papers documenting similar things in different ways. Once those papers are out there, suddenly debunking them becomes interesting. But you can’t really assess the state of knowledge on something like this until both sides of the academic incentive structure have played out. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Similarly, as I mentioned last week there is this </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/52d0ccfe-91cd-4ff1-b963-3cd63bb11aa1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">ideologically freighted debate happening</a><span> about trends in American versus European living standards that hinges on the details of how Purchasing Power Parities are calculated. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I think eventually someone will compile detailed evidence on consumption volumes — square feet of housing, number of cars, access to medical care, etc. — and maybe get us to clarity on this. In this case, I think you can probably say that even if Paul Krugman is right about the direct impact on living standards, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a8cd2475-a4c2-4b64-84f8-9a7dab728c82?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Mario Draghi is still correct</a><span> that it’s bad for Europe to not have a competitive high-tech sector for reasons of geopolitics. But it would still be nice to know who’s right!</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Descriptive work is under-rated</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A related issue is that high-quality descriptive work is pretty under-rated. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Eric Zwick and Owen Zidar have a book coming out this fall called “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/975905fc-7077-4099-8bdf-5bb486422b3d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">The Everywhere Millionaire: Who Is Really Rich in America and How They Got There</a><span>” that I read in galleys and liked a lot. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s an unusual book because while it makes points that are policy-relevant, it’s not really a policy book. The main point is simply to document that while the very richest people in America tend to be founders of tech companies or star investors, there is a broader set of rich people who collectively hold a huge share of wealth and political power based on businesses that are pretty banal. They talk about owners of HVAC companies, successful dental practices, mid-sized restaurant groups, beer distributors, auto dealerships, and other boring companies. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Zwick and Zidar have a descriptive finding that doesn’t exactly debunk this but does somewhat change how I think about it. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">They point out that a large fraction of rich Americans are like me: They own a small business and are also a key employee of the small business that they own. If you look at our tax returns, Kate and I earn pretty modest salaries. As a result, our employer enjoys incredible profit margins. But our employer is just us! This is tax optimization, not corporate overlords exploiting their workers. Zwick and Zidar say about a third of the fall in labor share is due to this kind of tax consideration rather than real change. So, again, not a debunking but a relevant consideration. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Another descriptive point that I think is underappreciated, even though people are constantly talking about housing, is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b3f1e512-3523-43cc-b3c9-58395b688ef9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Kevin Erdmann’s point</a><span> that the growth in real estate wealth in the United States since 1980 is mostly scarcity-induced rent inflation rather than the result of new investment. We’re just bidding up the price of land because we’re not building enough housing and actually becoming poorer as a result. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There’s a lot of diffuse anxiety that actually taking decisive action to eliminate the scarcity would also eliminate a lot of paper wealth. But people would actually be richer on average. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">A lot of trends are fake</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">One point here is just that it’s harder than it should be to know the truth about things. The internet has put more information than ever at everyone’s fingertips and made it really easy to look things up. But just looking stuff up is actually less useful than you might think. Obtaining knowledge is still difficult. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That’s in part because there are a lot of biases in the system toward publishing and propagating “interesting” findings. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Saloni Dattani had a good roundup recently of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9103485d-bfb6-4d0b-bdc5-edc30bac4a12?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">major media trends</a><span> that it turned out were based on methodological issues. The huge rise in maternal mortality that sparked dozens of articles actually just reflected a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c1ef4e6f-3d00-4748-88c4-125588aaa653?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">change in how deaths are counted</a><span>; nothing new actually happened. Dattani also alerted me to a study indicating that the collapse in interstate mobility in the United States — something I definitely believed was real — is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cf499cc0-c181-437c-9739-e20a345b43f2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">mostly a methodological change</a><span>.   </span></p><p class="button-wrapper"
